content: Thyroid hormone should never be used as a treatment for obesity in individuals with normal thyroid function. It is not effective for weight loss in such cases and can lead to severe or life-threatening toxicity, particularly when combined with amphetamines such as benzphetamine, dextroamphetamine, or methamphetamine. Discuss the potential risks of this medication with your doctor. Thyroid hormone is a naturally occurring hormone produced by the body. When used appropriately, it is prescribed to treat the symptoms of hypothyroidism, a condition in which the thyroid gland does not produce sufficient thyroid hormone. Symptoms of hypothyroidism include fatigue, depression, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry skin, coarse hair, muscle cramps, difficulty concentrating, aches and pains, leg swelling, and increased sensitivity to cold. Thyroid hormone is also used to treat goiter, which is an enlargement of the thyroid gland. This medication belongs to a class of drugs known as thyroid agents and works by supplementing the thyroid hormone that the body normally produces. Thyroid medication is available in tablet form and is taken orally, usually once daily before breakfast. It is important to take it at the same time every day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take the medication exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency unless instructed by your doctor. Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and gradually increase it. While thyroid medication helps manage the symptoms of hypothyroidism, it does not cure the condition. It may take several weeks before you notice any improvement in your symptoms. To maintain symptom control, you will likely need to take this medication for the rest of your life. Continue taking it even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking thyroid medication, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to thyroid hormone, any other medications, pork, or any ingredients in the tablets. Ask your pharmacist for a list of ingredients if needed. Provide your doctor and pharmacist with a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and nutritional supplements you are taking or plan to take. Be sure to mention specific medications such as androgens (e.g., danazol, testosterone), anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), antidepressants, aprepitant, carbamazepine, diabetes medications, digoxin, efavirenz, estrogen, griseofulvin, human growth hormone, insulin, lovastatin, nevirapine, oral contraceptives containing estrogen, oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, prednisone), phenobarbital, phenytoin, potassium iodide, rifabutin, rifampin, ritonavir, salicylates (e.g., aspirin, choline magnesium trisalicylate, diflunisal, magnesium salicylate, salsalate), strong iodine solution, and theophylline. If you take cholestyramine or colestipol, take them at least 4 hours before taking thyroid medication. Similarly, if you take antacids, iron-containing medications or supplements, simethicone, or sucralfate, take them at least 4 hours before or after your thyroid medication. Inform your doctor if you are using herbal products, especially St. John’s wort. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had diabetes, osteoporosis, atherosclerosis, cardiovascular disease (e.g., high blood pressure, high cholesterol, angina, arrhythmias, heart attack), malabsorption disorders, adrenal or pituitary gland dysfunction, or kidney or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking thyroid medication, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking thyroid medication. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking this medication. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Inform your doctor if you miss two or more consecutive doses. Thyroid medication may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms and they persist or worsen: weight loss, uncontrollable shaking of a body part, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, hyperactivity, anxiety, irritability, mood swings, difficulty sleeping, flushing, increased appetite, fever, changes in menstrual cycle, muscle weakness, or temporary hair loss (especially in children during the first month of therapy). Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience rash, difficulty breathing or swallowing, chest pain, rapid or irregular heartbeat, swelling of the hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, excessive sweating, heat intolerance, nervousness, or seizures. If you experience any unusual problems while taking this medication, inform your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly. Consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor will order lab tests to monitor your response to the medication. Inform your doctor and lab personnel that you are taking thyroid medication before undergoing any tests. Thyroid tablets may have a strong odor, but this does not indicate spoilage or ineffectiveness. Learn the brand and generic names of your medication, and check it each time you refill your prescription. Do not switch brands without consulting your doctor or pharmacist, as different brands may contain slightly different amounts of the medication. Do not share your medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
